\chapter{Water and Rice}
\label{ch:ml-water-and-rice}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name water and rice in Malayalam, keeping raw ari apart from cooked cōṟu.}

Say veḷḷam and explain why it does not match Tamil's nīr, then split ari from cōṟu.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{വെള്ളം} \ml{അരി} \ml{ചോറ്}]{\ml{വെള്ളം}, \ml{അരി}, \ml{ചോറ്} — a different water-word, the same rice-words}

\label{lesson:ML-C15-vellam-ari}



\begin{quote}
For once, Malayalam's everyday word for something basic genuinely \textbf{doesn't} match Tamil's — even though water is about as basic as vocabulary gets.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{വെള്ളം}} (\emph{veḷḷam}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{water}\textquotedblright{} — and notably, this is \textbf{not} built on \emph{nīr} the way Tamil's \emph{taṇṇīr} is. Instead, \emph{veḷḷam} shares the \textbf{\ml{വെൾ}} (\emph{veḷ-}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bright, white}\textquotedblright{}) root you already met in \emph{veḷḷi}, \textquotedblleft{}silver/ Venus,\textquotedblright{} from the colors and days lessons — \emph{veḷḷam} originally meant something closer to \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{flood, deluge}\textquotedblright{} before becoming Malayalam's plain, everyday word for water. (\emph{Nīr} itself hasn't vanished from Malayalam — it survives inside compounds like \textbf{\ml{ഇളനീർ}} \emph{iḷanīr}, \textquotedblleft{}tender coconut water,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\ml{കണ്ണീർ}} \emph{kaṇṇīr}, \textquotedblleft{}tears\textquotedblright{} — it's just not the standalone everyday word anymore.)

\begin{cousinweb}
Rice, though, tells the familiar story:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{അരി}} (\emph{ari}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rice}\textquotedblright{} (raw grain) — closely matching Tamil \emph{arisi}.
  \item \textbf{\ml{ചോറ്}} (\emph{cōṟu}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cooked rice}\textquotedblright{} (the meal) — and here Malayalam actually \textbf{does} have a Tamil cognate: Tamil keeps its own native \textbf{\ta{சோறு}} (also \emph{cōṟu}), used alongside the Sanskrit-influenced \emph{sātam} as an everyday near-synonym. Malayalam simply made \emph{cōṟu} its main word, where Tamil more often reaches for \emph{sātam}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}veḷḷam\textquotedblright{} — water, NOT matching Tamil's neer
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ari\textquotedblright{} — raw rice, matching Tamil closely
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cōṟu\textquotedblright{} — cooked rice, Malayalam's own word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Malayalam's everyday water-word match Tamil's? (\textbf{No} — \emph{veḷḷam} shares the \emph{veḷ-} \textquotedblleft{}bright/white\textquotedblright{} root instead, originally meaning \textquotedblleft{}flood\textquotedblright{}; though \emph{nīr} itself survives in compounds like \emph{iḷanīr} and \emph{kaṇṇīr}.) Does its raw-rice word match Tamil's? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{ari} closely matches \emph{arisi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
